column2: The occupied administration now conducts its public business under British authority. English is the recognised language of government, and the privileges attached to official recognition no longer extend to the Boer community. The burghers retain their language, their farms and their district ties, but they find themselves governed as subjects of an administration whose institutions no longer recognise them as the country's political foundation. Court business, appointments and petitions become daily reminders of the change imposed at Pretoria. Resentment spreads through meetings and correspondence, strengthening the committees that demand the restoration of the republic. Crown officers must administer a country whose largest community increasingly sees obedience as submission.
Administer the territory under Crown authority.

The declaration of independence restores more than a name above the public offices. The republic once again recognises the burgher community as the foundation of its government, and the language and civic arrangements suspended under Crown rule return with the Volksraad. District officials recover their republican authority while the commandos assemble for the struggle ahead. Petitions have given way to a declaration, and the institutions of self-government must now endure the test of war.

The isolated British station at Kariba has proved impossible to sustain as a territorial possession. It stands beyond the adjoining imperial districts, within country claimed and administered by the local government. The presence of a distant trading party cannot settle the question of sovereignty. Officials have therefore withdrawn the station's territorial claim and returned the district to its former administration. Any renewed expedition must proceed through an established route and arrangements with the rulers of the interior.
